articles.title: Andy Burnham gets his first taste of EU dealmaking and seems hungry for more
articles.summary: The prime minister is learning how tough EU negotiations can be - but it won't deter him from seeking closer ties.
articles.body:
Andy Burnham has hailed his deal with the EU as a "good day for Britain" and a "good day for Europe".

In the hours before the prime minister spoke, it had become, if nothing else, a confusing day.

That confusion was unleashed by an EU official who briefed reporters in the morning that implementing the new arrangements on youth mobility, food exports and carbon emissions would be contingent on the government agreeing within six months to cut university tuition fees for Europeans studying in Britain.

That was later qualified by others in the EU - and straightforwardly disputed by the British government.

And for all that it dominated the morning, it did not ultimately dominate or particularly overshadow what was a warm press conference between the prime minister and his EU counterparts, Ursula von der Leyen and Antonio Costa.

The settled position appears to be that negotiations on student fees will continue into the next six months but on a separate track, or a "different sheet of paper" as von der Leyen put it.

This still carries some degree of political risk for Burnham, because if Britain agrees to reduce, let alone equalise, university fees that would be an economic hit for universities which would presumably end up being covered by the government.

And it may still be possible, though probably unlikely, that a deterioration in those negotiations could pollute the progress of today's agreements.

Conversely, expect Burnham and his ministers to talk up another area where negotiations will continue - on the UK not being affected by the EU's "Made in Europe" plans, an attempt by the bloc to protect its industries from Chinese competition.

Today's achievements and hiccups alike may quickly pale into insignificance anyway.

UK and EU agree new deal for food exports, youth mobility and emissions but student fee talks to continue

Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow

What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start?

At the dramatic conclusion of his first party conference speech as Labour leader in September - a moment he has been dreaming of for decades - the prime minister vowed to get closer to the EU.

Over the subsequent two months it has at times been a bit unclear how exactly he envisages that playing out and quite how far he is willing to go.

But focusing on the process risks obscuring the most important development, which is that the prime minister and the government are now unambiguously committed to Britain not only getting closer, but getting much closer to the EU.

There were two significant moments at today's summit in that regard.

First, Burnham said that the government had got as far as it could go with incremental deals with the EU, at least this side of a general election.

In other words, he has got as far as he believes is possible with the strategy he inherited from Sir Keir Starmer of getting closer to the EU within the confines of the post-Brexit architecture set out by Theresa May all those years ago, of Britain remaining outside the single market and the customs union.

That suggests that after two years of this, there will not be a third annual summit to unveil specific agreements designed to smooth post-Brexit issues affecting specific sectors.

Yet it does sound like there will be another summit next year - or, rather, an "informal brainstorming process" about potential options for future relations with the EU.

That sounds pretty nebulous, sure, but an event dedicated specifically to both sides discussing how to change the terms of Britain's arrangements with the EU is likely to become quite a big moment when it arrives.

Perhaps as importantly, von der Leyen made clear that the EU was embracing this event too.

That said, it does diminish the chances of major movement from Burnham towards embracing a specific model for the EU relationship in the intervening period.

And what of the domestic politics of this?

Britain's seventh prime minister in just over 10 years watched from Manchester as the fraught relationship with Europe wrecked the careers of so many of those predecessors.

Burnham's gamble is that this time it's different.

He believes that public regret about how Brexit has played out opens the political space for a far-reaching renegotiation.

Plenty of Labour MPs enthusiastically agree, and see this as the route to uniting the "progressive" vote at the next election too.

Some, especially those who represent Labour's former industrial heartlands, are a little more apprehensive.

This morning's confusion is a reminder that there is another element to this gamble.

Negotiating with Brussels, even if both sides believe progress is a "win-win", can be a fraught and complicated business.

Once he's on the other side of his brainstorm, can Burnham carry that off without getting bogged down and distracting from his government's other priorities?

On the day he became Labour leader in July, Burnham described it as the biggest change moment in British politics in 40 years.

He was talking principally about economic transformation.

But going to Brussels and getting what he wants without serious complications would be a pretty big change too.

articles.title: Catherine Zeta-Jones' daughter says parents warned her about 'nepo baby' label
articles.summary: Carys Douglas, 23, made her stage debut this year in Anton Chekhov's play, The Seagull, in the US.
articles.body:
Catherine Zeta-Jones's daughter has said her parents warned her people might have "preconceived notions" about her embarking on an acting career, as she shared her views on the "nepo baby" label.

Carys Douglas, 23, made her stage debut this year, playing the lead role of Nina in Anton Chekhov's The Seagull in Brooklyn, New York.

Zeta-Jones, who is married to Michael Douglas, son of Hollywood star Kirk, previously said the "nepo baby" term was "horrific" . It refers to children of famous parents perceived to have achieved riches and success off their parents' backs.

But the young actor said her parents taught her to build her "own identity" and she has learned how to deal with the "pressure".

During an interview with Elle Spain, Carys Douglas said her parents "do not hide" from her that people would have preconceived ideas about her.

"They taught me that building my own identity depended on me and no one else. It was my responsibility, and it still is.

"As time has gone on, I've come to understand that there are different ways to deal with that kind of pressure," she said.

Her father, star of hit 1980s films such as Wall Street and Fatal Attraction, recently stated that he is not a fan of the "nepo baby" label, calling it an "unfortunate title".

"I guess you could say that about any business. The same thing with Hollywood royalty. My father's father was a junkman," Douglas, 82, said, referring to Kirk, who was considered a Hollywood Golden Age icon.

Zeta-Jones, 57, from Mumbles, Swansea, also criticised the phrase, saying it was "horrible because these kids didn't ask to be born into this, they're finding their own way in life".

"You have to go with your dreams, your passion," Zeta-Jones said.

She added: "But they love it, and they're good. Otherwise, Michael and I would be the first to go, 'you know what? Maybe law school looks really good'."

Zeta-Jones' big break came when she landed a West End role in 42nd Street in 1987, before she became a household name in the UK in 1991 after starring in the ITV hit The Darling Buds Of May.

She has since become a global superstar, with roles in The Mask Of Zorro, Entrapment, Traffic and 2002's adaptation of Chicago, for which she won an Oscar for Best Supporting Actress.

The couple's children, Dylan and Carys, have both followed in their footsteps into acting.

Michael Douglas said his children have been performing "since they were in kindergarten".

"Every play, every show, summer theater camps, graduating... I mean, they've done so much work. It's unbelievable," he said.

Douglas and Zeta-Jones' children predominantly grew up in the US, but the family regularly travels to Wales, a place they are fond of.

Speaking to British Vogue last November, Carys Douglas said her summers were spent reading on her grandmother's sofa and travelling around the Gower Peninsula in Swansea.

"I feel so lucky that this is where I'm from," she told the magazine, reflecting on the "weird but magical places" scattered across the peninsula.

"Those beaches are some of the most beautiful in the world," she said.

She also spoke about her "theatrical" family's traditions, recalling how "there'd be lots of little competitions for singing and pantomime shows all summer".

"It's true, the Welsh love to sing," she added.

articles.title: US Senate passes bill to speed up energy project approvals
articles.summary: The legislation aims to lower energy bills by making energy project approvals faster and limiting court challenges.
articles.body:
The United States Senate has passed a bipartisan bill to speed up approvals for power plants, transmission lines and other energy projects as lawmakers face pressure to bring down electricity bills and meet growing demand fuelled by the growth of artificial intelligence.

The Senate voted 62-33 on Thursday as 15 Democrats, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, backed the bill and two Republicans voted against it.

President Donald Trump had urged senators to pass the measure and said he would sign the bill if it passes the House of Representatives.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act would shorten timelines for federal reviews for energy projects and limit how approvals may be challenged in court.

It would change several environmental laws, including the National Environmental Policy Act, which requires federal agencies to weigh a project’s environmental effects and gives the public a chance to weigh in before a project is approved.

The four senators who coauthored the bill, two from each party, argued that Americans are tired of paying high utility bills while projects that could lower them are stuck in the planning phase.

“We are going to make it easier to build in America again and make life more affordable for American families,” Republican Senator Mike Lee of Utah said.

Lee negotiated the deal with fellow Republican Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and Democratic Senators Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island.

The bill would also require large AI data centres to pay for more of the cost of upgrading power grids to serve their needs.

The vote came after rising electricity bills and opposition to data centres became major issues in the midterm elections this month. Democrats campaigned on promises to rein in the industry and swept to victory. They won control of both chambers of the new US Congress, which will convene on January 3. Until then, Republicans hold slim majorities in both chambers.

Industry groups representing both renewable energy developers and oil and gas companies backed the bill, saying current delays can stretch timelines by a decade or more.

Environmental groups, including the Sierra Club and the National Wildlife Federation, warned that the bill would weaken protections for water and wildlife and make it harder for communities to challenge project approvals.

Other groups said it would lead to more fossil fuel development.

“Make no mistake: This backroom deal will pave the way for even more fossil fuel projects like gas power plants for data centres, oil and gas pipelines and [liquefied natural gas] terminals while sacrificing fundamental and common-sense public health and environmental protections for communities across the US,” said Jen Duggan, executive director of the Environmental Integrity Project.

She called it a “gift to some of the biggest polluters in America”, arguing that any gains in renewable energy would be outweighed by emissions and pollution from the fossil fuel industry.

Critics also took issue with how quickly the bill was moving, arguing that it was being rushed through Congress.

Democratic Senator Maria Cantwell from Washington state said after meeting with tribal leaders that it would undermine tribal nations’ sovereignty and weaken protections for their water, land and wildlife.

She called for more time to consider those concerns and amend the bill.

Some Democrats who opposed the bill also argued the party should wait until January to push through stronger legislation that limits fossil fuel development while doing more to expand wind and solar power.

The Senate passed the measure without adopting amendments pushed by Oregon’s two senators, including one that would ban data centres on public land and another that would prevent the Trump administration from cancelling energy grants and other Democratic initiatives for “purely political purposes”.

articles.title: Qatar and Germany deepen strategic ties during emir’s Berlin visit
articles.summary: German chancellor says Qatar pledged $16.5bn in new investments as the two countries deepen defence and technology ties.
articles.body:
Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani has held talks with German leaders in Berlin on expanding defence and diplomatic cooperation, broadening a relationship long focused on trade and investment.

At a joint news conference with the emir on Friday, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Qatar had pledged an additional 15 billion euros ($16.5bn) in investment, while the two governments planned closer cooperation on security and technology.

Merz said the investment would strengthen cooperation in artificial intelligence (AI), computer chips and aviation. He also expressed Germany’s interest in developing defence industry partnerships with Qatar, while the two countries agreed to work together to improve protection against cyberattacks.

The discussions come as Qatar continues pushing for a diplomatic solution to end the US-Israel war on Iran, which has disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a major route for global oil and gas supplies.

Sheikh Tamim also held talks with German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, who proposed a regional security conference for the Middle East.

Their meeting on Friday covered efforts to end the Iran war and restore maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, according to a joint statement by both countries.

Steinmeier suggested bringing regional governments together to build trust and address security disputes.

The emir invited him to the Doha Forum, an international policy conference in Qatar on December 5–6, to discuss the proposal further with other countries.

At the emir’s news conference with Merz, the German leader acknowledged Qatar’s role in mediating between the US and Iran and called for the Strait of Hormuz to reopen permanently. He also urged Tehran to halt its military nuclear programme.

Sheikh Tamim stressed that “peace and sustainable peace and security can only be reached through a political agreement”, adding that dialogue is the only way forward. He also described Germany as an important partner.

Sheikha Alanoud bint Hamad Al Thani, a fellow at the Middle East Council for Global Affairs, a regional research institute, told Al Jazeera in Berlin that the relationship had previously been driven mainly by commerce.

“But now we’re seeing a strategic dialogue,” she said, pointing to increasingly similar security concerns, including drone attacks on Qatar and hybrid warfare threats facing European countries.

That shift builds on a 2023 agreement to establish formal strategic talks between the two countries. Sheikh Tamim told Steinmeier on Friday that Qatar wanted the first round to take place, according to Qatar’s state news agency, QNA.

articles.title: Jarrow pigeon 'strung up like puppet' in horrific attack
articles.summary: The pigeon was found in Jarrow and is now recovering with an animal rescue charity in Sunderland.
articles.body:
Warning: This article contains details of animal abuse

A pigeon has made a full recovery after it was strung up and turned into a living puppet "like Pinocchio", an animal rescue charity has said.

The bird, which was found abandoned and unable to move by a dog walker in Jarrow, had its wings bound in tape and was attached to a stick using fishing wire.

The woman, who was alerted to the stranded animal by her dog, brought the bird to Pawz for Thought in Sunderland to be cared for.

The charity's director, Lorraine Thornton, said the pigeon had been left "kind of mummified" and had been "just sitting there waiting for death" before it was found.

"They'd got a twig and tied off all of the fishing wire to the twig to make a puppet, almost like Pinocchio," she said.

Thornton said it was one of the most "horrific things she had seen" because it meant someone had sat and taken the time to torture the animal before leaving it to die.

She said the team removed the tape using vegetable oil and were surprised to find the bird had no injuries.

He is now living in one of the charity's aviaries.

A spokesperson for the RSPCA said animal abuse can cause "immense suffering and can have devastating consequences for both individual animals and local wildlife populations".

"We're really grateful to the team at Pawz for Thought for the work they've done to nurse this pigeon back to health and we'd urge anyone with first-hand knowledge about this awful incident to contact the RSPCA," they said.

"We're deeply concerned by the growing number of these sorts of reports involving deliberate cruelty towards wild birds which feel pain, fear and distress."

The RSPCA said there were 359 incidents of cruelty towards birds in England between July and August 2025 - the highest figure in five years and up from 179 reports in the same period in 2024.

The charity said many of the incidents involved "lethal weapons" such as catapults, slingshots and airguns.

articles.title: Rao and Patil: The two desis behind Anthropic's bang and buck
articles.summary: TOI Correspondent From Washington: At a time when America is debating whether it has room for immigrants amid MAGA-driven xenophobia, there was sweet
articles.body: TOI Correspondent From Washington: At a time when America is debating whether it has room for immigrants amid MAGA-driven xenophobia, there was sweet irony in two executives of Indian-origin occupying the C-suite of Anthropic as it made its historic market debut on Thursday.Krishna Rao, the company's chief financial officer (CFO), whose financial stewardship helped turn an AI start-up into a corporate juggernaut, was on stage with the seven co-founders at the Nasdaq bell-ringing. In the background, as they generally tend to be, was Anthropic’s chief technology officer (CTO) Rahul Patil, who is responsible for the engineering and infrastructure powering its formidable artificial intelligence ambitions.The two men, both products of Indian middle-class backgrounds and now members of the upper echelons of America's tech elite, represent different routes to the same extraordinary destination. Raised in California in a family with modest means, Krishna Rao was encouraged to aim high without assuming that money would be readily available. His elder brother chose an in-state college so that the family could afford to send Rao to Harvard, after which he went on to Yale Law School.Born and raised in Bengaluru, Patil had a different trajectory, attending Baldwin School and St Joseph's in Bengaluru before earning a computer science engineering degree from PES University, then known as PES Institute of Technology. He moved to the U.S in 2003 for a master's degree in computer science at Arizona State University and later earned an MBA from the University of Washington in Seattle.Both had stellar careers before hitting the high spot in Anthropic. After graduating summa cum laude in economics from Harvard in 2005, Rao worked as a consultant at Bain & Company in San Francisco and New Delhi, and then moved into private equity after a law degree from Yale, becoming a principal at Blackstone. He later became the global head of corporate and business development at Airbnb, helping steer the company through the pandemic and its 2020 stock-market listing. He joined Anthropic in May 2024 as its first CFO.Patil spent nearly a decade at Microsoft after his MBA from U-W, then worked at Amazon Web Services, where he led engineering associated with large-scale data-processing infrastructure, and subsequently held senior leadership positions at Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. His last major assignment before Anthropic was at Stripe, the payments giant processing more than a trillion dollars in annual transactions, where he served as the CTO.Also in the Anthropic mix are two other execs of Indian-origin: Sid Bidasaria, who is the technology builder behind Claude Code, and Neil Shah, who is Chairman of Anthropic's Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT), which is mandated to ensure that Anthropic’s development of advanced AI remains aligned with its mission of benefiting humanity.For Rao, the IPO was also a spectacular money-spinner. The final SEC disclosures show that he held 9,497,900 shares before the offering. He sold approximately 1.66 million shares in the IPO, retaining 7,837,991, which makes him the largest disclosed non-founder individual shareholder, behind Anthropic's seven co-founders. At Thursday's closing price, that holding was worth about $762 million. Unlike Rao’s shareholding, which is disclosed in Anthropic’s IPO documents, individual shareholding of other Indian execs is not revealed, but there is little doubt they are all multi-millionaire.But more than the lolly, they have underscored the larger paradox in contemporary American politics. At a time MAGA mania has made immigration, foreign workers and the H-1B visa contentious subjects, they have shown that Indian-Americans remain conspicuously at the forefront of the tech primacy that Washington desires for the United States.You use AI every day. articles.title: 10 years after divisive Brexit referendum, UK weighs a ‘Breturn’ to the EU
articles.summary: Prime Minister Andy Burnham returns from the UK-EU summit with a potential new deal and a new start.
articles.body:
A decade after the narrow vote to leave the EU, the United Kingdom is showing every sign of buyer’s remorse.

For many, the bitterly fought contest over the referendum on whether to leave the EU was unpleasant and divisive.

Couples and families reportedly split over where they stood on the referendum. Each side of the debate – Leave and Remain – became a cipher for how people saw themselves and their country in a changing world.

As the campaign unfolded amid accusations of foreign influence and dirty tricks, the murder of a politician , a debate over economics and political sovereignty, a visceral fight intensified over identity, belonging and competing visions of what it meant to be British.

Critics and pro-Brexit slammed various exit deals that successive governments negotiated with Brussels as somehow a betrayal of what had originally been a binary choice.

The EU, the trading bloc the UK sat uneasily within for nearly half a century, remains the country’s biggest trading partner.

On Friday, in a joint news conference with Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, following the latest UK-EU summit in Brussels, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham hailed the first in a series of expected deals with the EU as rebuilding “the bridges that were broken all those years ago”.

The agreements, which cover three main areas – easing trade restrictions, expanding opportunities for young people to live and work across borders, and addressing carbon levies – were characterised by Burnham as “a good deal for Britain” and regarded as first steps towards bringing the UK back into the EU’s orbit.

Some in the UK believe that leaving the single market and customs union brought little tangible benefit while creating additional paperwork, border checks and barriers to trade with the UK’s largest export market. Others have no regrets about leaving the bloc.

According to polling expert Sir John Curtice, surveys show an average of 62 percent favour rejoining, against 38 percent for staying out, once undecided respondents are excluded.

“Whatever the nuances, the UK public are certainly in a different place on the EU than [they were] in 2016,” he told Al Jazeera.

According to some analysts, the government – which is not bound by a single written constitution – could, with the EU’s agreement, begin the process of rejoining without holding another referendum, or even including the commitment in an election manifesto.

However, doing so would inevitably be politically difficult and, according to Professor Curtice, almost certain to be highly unpopular.

“The Brexit referendum in 2016 was not legally binding,” Sionaidh Douglas-Scott, the chair in Law at Queen Mary University of London, wrote by email. “Legally, it could have been ignored altogether. But it was thought to be politically unacceptable to ignore the public’s vote in the referendum. And political parties can ignore their election manifesto pledges at their peril,” she said, referring to parties’ reliance on public trust to support any agenda.

“I suspect Burnham might be tempted to have a referendum on the issue of rejoining the EU, feeling that public opinion had changed sufficiently to render a rejoin vote likely, although that’s by no means certain,” she said. “Some senior members of the [governing Labour] party … clearly feel that rejoining should be a manifesto pledge. So, politically, steps might be taken to make it more acceptable.”

Meanwhile, questions remained over the terms on which the UK might rejoin the bloc, whether it would be required to adopt the euro – a prospect it had previously resisted – and what form the EU itself might take following elections in some of its most influential member states, including France, Germany and Spain.

Polling suggests a distinction between support for closer relations with the EU as opposed to support for full membership.

While some surveys put support for rejoining at about 35 percent when closer ties were offered as an alternative, Curtice said support for closer relations was often less firmly held.

“Much of that support is soft – people say they somewhat support rather than strongly support” closer ties, he explained. By contrast, around half of those supporting rejoining the EU say they “strongly support” it, suggesting a deeper commitment to that option.

Similarly, at home, many of the more prominent figures of the original campaign to leave Europe have resurfaced and appear to be marshalling their forces against any return or realignment.

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, one of Brexit’s most prominent campaigners, returned to Brussels on Thursday to oppose the prime minister’s efforts.

Other figures associated with the Leave campaign have also re-emerged, including former Prime Minister Boris Johnson and his former cabinet ally, Michael Gove, now a magazine editor. They have revived loosely sourced claims about the financial cost of rejoining the EU – or even of having remained a member. The campaign group Stay Out, for instance, puts the annual cost at 39.3 billion pounds (approximately $51.4bn), equivalent to 750 million pounds (about $982m) a week.

“I think we should think about two things when we think about Brexit and the potential to rejoin: trauma and salience,” Anand Menon, professor at King’s College London and director of UK in a Changing Europe, said. “Some people felt traumatised by the first debate and don’t want to revisit it. At the same time, the issue has lost its salience. The public don’t consider it one of the main issues facing the country,” he said.

“If you cast your mind back to 2016, those supporting Leave, like Nigel Farage, took the EU, which the public never really thought about, and linked it in the public’s mind to something they absolutely did: immigration.

“If Burnham is going to try to get the sort of energy he’ll need to see the process through, he’s going to need to do something similar, though what, I don’t know.”

articles.title: NIA probes 'Indian footprint' in flydubai pilot stabbing case, seeks UAE assistance
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The National Investigation Agency (NIA) is probing possible Indian links in the mid-air stabbing of a flydubai pilot and has sought documents
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The National Investigation Agency (NIA) is probing possible Indian links in the mid-air stabbing of a flydubai pilot and has sought documents from the UAE as well as permission to question some people there, news agency PTI reported, citing NIA director General Rakesh Aggarwal.The probe is examining whether the accused Omani first officer had any Indian connections, including people in his circle who could have been linked to the alleged attack, Aggarwal said on Friday."We have already sent a mutual legal assistance request to the UAE asking for copies of certain documents and also permission to examine some persons in the UAE. So, we are waiting for a response from them," Aggarwal said.The request has been sent under the Mutual Legal Assistance Treaty (MLAT), which enables countries to cooperate in criminal investigations.The NIA is also examining the first officer's background, including reports that he studied in Australia or the UK, and is looking into whom he came in contact with during his time there."So whom did he come in contact with? Are there any Indian footprints of his friend circle who could be lurky? So there are various issues," Aggarwal said, adding that the agency would proceed with its investigation once it receives the documents and information from the UAE.The NIA registered a case in October to investigate the larger conspiracy behind the September 30 mid-air attack on Captain Smit Machchhar aboard flydubai flight FZ 1073, which was travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv.According to the agency's FIR, the Omani first officer allegedly stabbed Captain Machchhar mid-air in an apparent attempt to hijack the aircraft or cause it to crash. The incident took place in Saudi airspace near the Jordan-Saudi Arabia border.The agency has invoked Section 3 of the Anti-Hijacking Act, 2016, and provisions of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, including Section 16, which deals with punishment for terrorist acts.Captain Machchhar sustained critical injuries in the attack. The aircraft, carrying 174 passengers and six crew members, was landed safely at Prince Sultan bin Abdulaziz Airport in Tabuk, northwestern Saudi Arabia, by the other pilots on board. The first officer was arrested by Saudi authorities.The NIA's probe is now focused on establishing the larger conspiracy behind the attack, including whether there were any Indian links or individuals connected to the accused's network.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘ICJ ruling made world finally record our pain & loss,’ say Rohingya refugees at Bangladesh camp
articles.summary: After the landmark judgment by International Court of Justice (ICJ), terming the killings of Rohingyas by Myanmar junta forces as “genocide”, displaced
articles.body: After the landmark judgment by International Court of Justice (ICJ), terming the killings of Rohingyas by Myanmar junta forces as “genocide”, displaced community members living in the world’s largest refugee settlement of Kutupalong camp in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh, hailed the verdict as a “global acknowledgement of their unparalleled suffering, pain and loss”.Speaking to TOI over phone on Friday, Ak Mohammed Sadek, 27, a Rohingya who arrived at the Cox’s Bazar camp with his mother and six siblings in 2017, said that everyone at the settlement were nervously following the news on their radios.“We’ve suffered for a decade… The world has now finally recorded our immense pain. This strengthens our hope of returning home one day -- with dignity and honour,” said Sadek, who claimed to have witnessed his father shot dead and an aunt burnt alive after rape in 2017. He was a Class 10 student at that time and lost at least nine members of his family.Sadek added that he had to run for his life from Dhumsay Para village in Myanmar’s Rakhine state.“After my father, I lost my mother to a serious ailment at the camp. She was heartbroken after seeing what she shouldn’t have,” the 27-year-old said.Rohingya refugees gathered on Friday in Cox’s Bazar refugee camp during the event of UNGA president Khalilur Rahman. (PC: Ak Mohammed Sadek/Cox’s Bazar) Twenty-six-year-old Sanaullah Omar fled his village with his parents and two siblings that same year to be at the refugee camp. “The UN top court’s judgment on Thursday has given us the will to live and fight again,” he said, adding that “the violence we suffered in 2017 haunts me and others all the time. It flashes before my eyes.”Omar’s father was a village head who saw his dwellings burnt down. “We walked on empty stomachs through dense forests and travelled on a boat for around five days to reach Cox’s Bazar,” he added. After completing his classes 9 and 10 at the refugee camp school, Omar now works as a teacher at an UNICEF-run school within the settlement.Laila Begam’s fate and destiny seemed to be similar to those of Sadek and Omar, both much younger than her. Like them, she escaped death with her family of 10 that year.“Today is an emotional day for me. Though I don’t understand much of the court ruling, I only know that they (ICJ) have told the world that a crime like that should not go unpunished. Since the ruling, I’ve been praying for the departed souls...,” said Begam, with several pauses as her voice shook with emotion.She told TOI: “I’m 65. But, I still hope I’ll see my home in Myanmar some day.”According to data on the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees’ website, the Cox’s Bazar refugee settlement hosts around 11.7 lakh Rohingya refugees who fled violence in Myanmar.Ak Mohammed Sadek (centre) with other Rohingya refugees at Cox’s Bazar on Friday. (PC: Ak Mohammed Sadek/Cox’s Bazar) Meanwhile, Bangladesh minister of foreign affairs, Khalilur Rahman, who holds the position of president of 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), visited the settlement at Cox’s Bazar on Friday.Terming the ICJ verdict as “final and unequivocal”, he said: “While the judgment can’t bring back the dead or heal everyone, the truth is, justice begins now. After considering all the evidence and hearing Myanmar’s arguments, ICJ made it clear that what was done to the Rohingyas in 2017 was a genocide.”Myanmar govt spokesperson, Khaing Khaing Soe, meanwhile said in capital Naypyidaw that his country was “unjustly accused”. He added: “This decision is not unanimous; it is not fair.”ICJ said on Thursday that “mass executions of men and boys, widespread rape and sexual violence against Rohingya women and burning or razing of hundreds of villages” were carried out during the so-called clearance operations in Myanmar.You use AI every day. articles.title: Orphaned baby marmoset named after UK detective who saved him
articles.summary: Detective Constable Gino Ferrara normally spends his days investigating rape and serious sexual offences on London’s streets. But on November 11, the detective encountered a tiny, scared, baby monkey trapped in a south London shed.
articles.body: Detective Constable Gino Ferrara normally spends his days investigating rape and serious sexual offences on London’s streets. But on November 11, the detective encountered a tiny, scared, baby monkey trapped in a south London shed. “When I saw the marmoset I was shocked. The yard where he was being kept smelt awful, like feces, and there were dogs running loose and barking constantly,” Det. Con. Ferrara said in a press release from the UK Metropolitan Police. “You could hear this little monkey screaming. We could just tell he was scared; he looked shocked and confused,” Det. Con. Ferrara added. Officers were at the property following a warrant by the Met’s Trident unit in October connected with a separate investigation into the alleged possession of a firearm. They discovered the 5-month-old marmoset locked in a bird cage in a shed and passed the intelligence onto wildlife specialists. That’s when Det. Con. Ferrara, who volunteers his time with wildlife crime officers, quickly arranged to get help from a local sanctuary called Monkey World. He and Dr. Alison Cronin from the rescue went out to the property and couldn’t believe what they saw. Dr. Cronin says she was surprised the baby marmoset was still alive because “he is so young and was left on his own in a cold garden shed in a bird cage.” “It must have been lonely, scary, and very cold, especially for a youngster who should still be carried by his parents,” Dr. Cronin added, according to the press release. The property’s occupants willingly surrendered the monkey to officers claiming they were just taking care of him for a friend, according to police. He was then taken to Monkey World and introduced to an adult black-tufted marmoset named Minty. He instantly tried to climb onto her back as if she were his mother. Now that baby monkey has a name — Gino — after the detective who changed his life. “We are so pleased for Gino that he has found a mum in Minty and that he is now getting the specialist care that he needs,” Dr. Cronin said. “To see that I’ve played a part in ensuring Gino has gone to a good home makes me feel very proud,” Det. Con. Ferrara said. So far no arrests have been made but an animal welfare investigation is underway.

articles.title: Zohran Mamdani tears Achilles while playing soccer against NYC press corps
articles.summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani will be hobbling in a walking boot for at least the next six weeks, saying he forgot that he’s on the doorstep of middle age and tore his Achilles while playing soccer.
articles.body: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani will be hobbling in a walking boot for at least the next six weeks, saying he forgot that he’s on the doorstep of middle age and tore his Achilles while playing soccer. The first-term mayor of America’s biggest city paid a heavy price for scoring a goal in a friendly match between City Hall and the New York City press corps Thursday night. Mamdani showed up on crutches to Friday’s news conference announcing the plan to close the Rikers Island jail. He admitted that he didn’t properly stretch. “For those who don’t know, we played a friendly game against the press corps last night, soccer, which we won 10-5 and I scored a goal soon after getting on the pitch,” the Big Apple’s chief executive and devoted Arsenal supporter told reporters. “I forgot that I was 35, and soon after, I tore my Achilles,” Mamdani said. “I will be in a boot for six to eight weeks. I will play soccer in about nine months.” The link between middle-aged weekend warriors and ruptured Achilles tendons is well known. “Middle-aged adults doing sports activities are more likely to get this kind of injury,” according to the Columbia University Irving Medical Center. “Tears also happen in older adults.”

articles.title: Carville calls out 'ultimate urban progressive' Pramila Jayapal for Jeffries comment, urges 'self-education'
articles.summary: James Carville called Rep. Pramila Jayapal the "ultimate urban progressive" on a podcast, blasting her "short rope" remark about Hakeem Jeffries.
articles.body: Democratic strategist James Carville called out Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., during a podcast on Thursday over her remarks directed at House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., calling her the "ultimate urban progressive." "But in terms of Hakeem being speaker, there was an incident that illustrates just how clueless and how the progressive urban left has no idea of what the Democratic Party is," Carville said during a "Politicon" podcast. "Let me refer you to Congresswoman Pramila Jayapal, she's from Seattle, she is the ultimate urban progressive, and she said of Speaker-to-be Hakeem Jeffries, who is actually a Black person, that he needs to be on a short rope. This woman is so f---ing ignorant of Black history." Jayapal said in an interview with Talking Points Memo last week that Jeffries would have "a relatively short rope to show that kind of urgency" as speaker. Jayapal said she wanted his help to secure votes for Medicare for All. HAKEEM JEFFRIES WINS OVERWHELMING SPEAKER-DESIGNATE VOTE AS PROGRESSIVES' REVOLT FALLS FLAT She later clarified on X that she meant "a short window to act" and condemned the use of lynching imagery to intimidate anyone. Jeffries was elected to become the next House speaker on Wednesday. He brushed off the "no" votes from progressives after winning the votes. JEFFRIES SURVIVES DEM VOTE TO SECURE SPEAKER POSITION AS PROGRESSIVE RESISTANCE CLOUDS HIS CHANCES Carville said that Jayapal was, "So f---ing ignorant of the history of the country that she comes from." "It's a rather sensitive word to a lot of people, not just Black people, to be talking about that. There's a horrific history in this country, Ms. Jayapal, which you're not aware of, of what I guess you would call it, extrajudicial lynchings. Yeah, that's what we're talking about. And I think it's very important that these people submit themselves to self-education," Carville added. DEMOCRATIC LAWMAKERS ERUPT AFTER ANTI-ISRAEL JOURNALIST CALLS HAKEEM JEFFRIES AN ‘AIPAC MONKEY’ IN VIRAL RANT Jayapal told Talking Points Memo in the interview published on Nov. 10 that she wanted to see a new Senate leader, but pointed out there were no challenges to Jeffries. She said a challenger would have changed everyone's calculus. "I think he will have a relatively short rope to show that kind of urgency and perhaps abandon some of the caution that everybody notes as one of his qualities," Jayapal said of Jeffries. "He is cautious and sometimes that can be good, but in a moment where you have this kind of anger and need, demand for bold reform, in order for him to be successful and to hold a speakership, he’s going to have to be able to respond very quickly to that." CHARLAMAGNE BLASTS AOC FOR ‘BEATING AROUND THE BUSH,’ PRESSES PROGRESSIVES ON BACKING HAKEEM JEFFRIES Democratic strategist Kaivan Shroff told Fox News Digital in a statement, "I don’t think Jayapal was making a lynching reference, and she clarified what she meant. But ‘short rope’ was an incredibly careless phrase to use about the man poised to become the first Black speaker. Carville overreaches if the argument is that criticizing Jeffries is somehow off-limits. The more interesting problem is that parts of the far left have a real blind spot when Black Democrats do not fit their preferred story about ‘the base.’" Shroff added, "Black Democrats somehow disappear from the picture whenever the far left finds them inconvenient and when you call it out, you get accused of ‘identity politics.’ You can challenge Jeffries all you want. Just don’t pretend the loudest people online are the whole Democratic Party." HAKEEM JEFFRIES CONFRONTED ON 'YOU'RE NEXT' CHANTS FOLLOWING NY DEMOCRATIC SOCIALIST VICTORIES Carville previously told Fox News Digital the progressive movement is insular, saying its acceptance of political allies depended on whether it considered them part of the group. "I find that whole, you know, progressive whole thing very exclusionary in nature," Carville said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "They only want you if they think you’re one of them, you know. I’m not a fan." Jayapal and Jeffries' offices did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE Jayapal praised Jeffries over a commitment to expand Medicare on Tuesday, according to Politico. Jayapal said, "That is a really important step towards Medicare for All." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News' CJ Womack contributed to this report.

articles.title: Why I love the retro Tin Can phone for my kid, plus, what it can’t do
articles.summary: Is the Tin Can kids’ phone worth $100? A mom tested the screen-free Wi-Fi “landline” with her 5-year-old for a month. Here’s what she liked and what to know.
articles.body: Back when I was a kid, if I wanted to call a friend, I had to use the corded phone in our kitchen. I can still remember stretching that coiled cord as far as it would go so I could squeeze into the pantry for a little privacy. It was annoying back then. Now that I’m a parent, I can see how good it was for me. It kept me in the middle of family life, I wasn’t tempted to disappear into a screen, and my parents could keep tabs on what was going on in my life. I’ve been thinking about this a lot because, lately, my nearly 6-year-old has been asking to FaceTime friends and family pretty frequently, which usually means borrowing my phone and then getting distracted by everything else on it. That matters more than it may seem: A study of more than 50,000 U.S. children published in January 2026 found that kids ages 6 to 17 who spent four or more hours a day on screens had 61% higher odds of depression and 45% higher odds of anxiety. I’m not the only one thinking about the perils of screentime. Every parent I know is trading ideas for keeping their kids off screens a little longer, and lately a lot of those conversations have turned to the Tin Can, a Wi-Fi landline made just for kids. So when I got the chance to test one, the timing couldn’t have been better. But is a $100 retro phone actually worth it, or is it just a cute novelty? Keep reading to learn what I found after trying it with my daughter for more than a month. What is the Tin Can? The Tin Can looks like a classic corded landline, but it actually runs on your home Wi-Fi. Parents set it up and manage it through a companion app that is available for iPhone and Android. You choose exactly who your kid can call and who can call them, so strangers can’t reach out through this line. Calls between two Tin Cans are free and unlimited, with no subscription. If you want your kid to be able to call Grandma’s cell phone or a friend whose family doesn’t have a Tin Can, you’ll need the Party Line Plan, which costs $10 a month. Each phone comes with one free month of the plan. What I like about the Tin Can I tested the Tin Can for more than a month with my nearly 6-year-old as the main user. We set it up in our hallway and added a handful of approved contacts, including grandparents and a few classmates. Here’s what stood out. It’s genuinely screen-free This is the whole point, and it delivers. There are no apps, no games or videos to get pulled into, just a handset and buttons. When my kid wanted to talk to a friend, the conversation was the only thing happening — it felt like the early ‘90s all over again. I control who can call Every contact goes through the parent app first, so only people I’ve approved can call in or out. I also set calling hours so the phone goes quiet during early morning hours, dinner and bedtime. The app’s call log lets me see who my kid has talked to without hovering over the conversation. Setup was simple The phone plugs into a regular outlet and connects to Wi-Fi through the app. There’s no phone jack or landline service to deal with. Between downloading the app, adding contacts and plugging in the phone, setup took about 15 minutes. One thing to know: it only works on a 2.4GHz Wi-Fi network, which most home routers support. It builds real phone skills Kids today rarely learn how to answer a phone, say who’s calling or leave a message. The Tin Can’s voicemail and speed dial gave my kid a low-stakes way to practice. I even incorporated ways for her to practice interacting with people over the phone — for example, I had her call the local library to find out what time they closed. I hadn’t thought about it until we got the phone, but this type of thing was a given when I was a kid. But, now, with the internet, kids aren’t forced to rely on human interaction to get the info they need — a skill I’d like to make sure my kids have. It’s just plain fun The Tin Can comes in bright colors with playful names, like Landline Lemon and Later Alligator Lilac. It has a corded handset, and the kids can record a custom voicemail greeting. Because I keep my cell phone on vibrate, I also realized my daughter had never gotten the opportunity to get excited about an incoming call. Having a phone that actually rang turned out to be thrilling for her. Potential drawbacks to keep in mind The best features cost extra Calls between Tin Cans are free, but that only helps if your kid’s friends have one too. To call regular cell phones or landlines, you’ll need the Party Line Plan, which costs $10 per month. That’s about $120 a year on top of the $100 phone. It’s only as useful as your network of Tin Can families The more friends who have one, the more value you get. Because even though you can call other phones if you have a plan, kids are more likely to call one another if they do not have to go through a parent’s cell phone. Thankfully, I know a number of families with Tin Can phones. If you’re the first family in your circle, it may feel quiet at first. It’s not a backup emergency phone Calling 911 is free and always on. But because the phone runs on Wi-Fi and wall power, it likely will not work during a power or internet outage. Tin Can recommends keeping another way to reach emergency services. Who is the Tin Can for? The Tin Can is a nice option for parents who want their kids to stay connected with friends and family but aren’t ready to hand over a smartphone or tablet. It’s a great fit for early elementary school kids like mine who are just starting to want their own social lives. It’s also good for families who want an easy way for kids to call their grandparents. If your kid’s friends already have Tin Cans, it’s an easy yes. If not, plan on budgeting for the Party Line Plan, or recruit a few other families to buy one too. Judging by how many parents I know are talking about it, that may not be hard. Is the Tin Can worth it? After a month with the Tin Can, both my daughter and I are fans. Her favorite part is having a phone that’s all her own: she calls her grandparents and friends without having to borrow mine. My favorite part is what it’s teaching her. Using a landline means learning phone etiquette most kids don’t pick up anymore, like saying hello and asking who’s calling, waiting her turn to talk and ending the call politely. Watching her figure that out took me right back to stretching the cord into our pantry, and I loved that she’s getting a version of that experience. That said, I’d keep expectations realistic. The Tin Can is a great way to stay connected without a screen, but it doesn’t replace screened devices. It won’t stand in for a tablet, and it hasn’t made the fight over screen time any easier in our house. She still asks for the iPad. I also suspect it has a shelf life: right now a phone of her own feels like a big deal, but as she gets older and her friends start getting devices that text, I expect the Tin Can will appeal to her less. For now, it gives her a screen-free option for one specific thing she used to need my phone for. Other kid-friendly phones on the market While Tin Can is arguably the most popular phone for kids on the market right now, there are a number of other options available. Waffle Home is a screen-free first phone for kids ages 5 to 12. It has no display or internet access and makes calls over your home Wi-Fi, but only to contacts parents approve in the Waffle Hub app. It has the option of being cordless, so kids can chat anywhere in the house, and it supports voice notes, caller ID, emergency calling and quiet hours. The brand also offers the Waffle Go, which is more like a screenless cell phone. The Pinwheel Home Classic is a screen-free landline for kids, with a chunky retro handset that comes in pink, black or white. Similar to the Tin Can and Waffle, it works over Wi-Fi with no phone jack needed, and kids can call only the contacts parents approve. Calls to other Pinwheel Home phones are free, while calls to outside numbers require a subscription. MyPhone by Ooma is a screen-free corded phone for kids from a longtime internet home phone company. It runs over your home Wi-Fi and calls only the contacts parents add to their “Trusted Circle” via the app. Parents can set quiet hours and review call logs, and its address-based 911 service sends text alerts to family if your child ever dials for help. Want more from NBC Selected? Sign up for our newsletter, The Selection, and shop smarter. Why trust NBC Selected? I am a commerce editor at NBC Selected and a journalist who regularly covers tech and lifestyle, among other topics. I have recently written about red light therapy and sleep, wellness tech brand HigherDose and more. I am also a mom of two — a nearly 6-year-old and nearly 2-year-old. For this story, I let my daughter test the Tin Can phone for over a month and took notes on how the experience went. Catch up on NBC Selected’s in-depth coverage of tech and tools, wellness and more, and follow us on Facebook, Instagram, X and TikTok to stay up to date.

articles.title: Javits Frimpong Ghanaian boy killed in US remembered at funeral
articles.summary: At the funeral for the 15-year-old who was fatally shot last month, Mamdani spoke alongside the boy's father and civil rights leaders.
articles.body:
A 15-year-old Ghanaian boy who was killed in the US last month was remembered as a hard-working student with dreams of becoming a doctor, as his father, New York City's mayor and civil rights leaders gave eulogies during his funeral on Friday.

Javits Frimpong was shot and killed while walking to school in the Bronx. His death has sparked outrage in both Ghana and the US, and reignited debates about gun violence in America.

"Javits deserved so much better and so do every single one of you," Mayor Zohran Mamdani said. "Though he was only a New Yorker for a short time, New York City will forever be proud to call Javits one of our own."

Frimpong moved to the US about a year before the shooting.

"I worked hard to bring you from Ghana to America because I wanted you to have opportunities, a better future, and a chance to achieve everything that you dreamed of," his father, Thomas Frimpong, said.

His mother was granted an emergency visa from Ghana to mourn her son at Friday's funeral service, following Mamdani's lobbying of President Donald Trump earlier this month.

Earlier this month, she told the BBC that she wanted "justice for my son", a sentiment echoed at Friday's service.

Frimpong was chased down and shot on 29 October. He was taken to a local hospital, where he was pronounced dead.

Police have said three teenage boys were involved in the shooting. A 17-year-old has been arrested and charged with murder, and will be tried as an adult. Police are still searching for the other two.

"Gun violence is never the answer," Ben Crump, an attorney representing the family, said at the funeral as he vowed to seek justice for Frimpong.

Ghana's government has condemned the killing and said it would follow the case closely to ensure justice was achieved.

It has urged US authorities to conduct a thorough investigation and said it was ready to provide legal and consular support to ensure the perpetrators were brought to justice.

articles.title: Gérard Depardieu and French author Michel Houellebecq investigated over sexual allegations
articles.summary: A judicial investigation was launched after a complaint was filed last year over "allegations of a sexual nature".
articles.body:
Warning: this story contains graphic content

French authorities are investigating disgraced actor Gérard Depardieu and the author Michel Houellebecq over "allegations of a sexual nature", a source with knowledge of the investigation says.

The confirmation comes after reports in French media that the two were accused of being involved in a "gang rape" on the set of the film Thalasso in 2018 by an actress.

The source told the BBC that a judicial investigation was launched after a complaint was filed in May 2025.

Depardieu has already separately been convicted of unrelated sexual assaults. The BBC has contacted Depardieu's lawyers and Houellebecq, an acclaimed French author and occasional actor, for comment.

The actress, who has not been named publicly, accused Depardieu of penetration without consent and Houellebecq of forcing her to perform oral sex, in an interview with Mediapart, a French investigative site which first reported the allegations.

She told the outlet that none of this had been written into the script, and that she experienced "profound humiliation" and "unspeakable shame".

French law stipulates as of 2025 that all sexual acts performed without consent constitute rape.

The film's director, Guillaume Nicloux, has been accused of being complicit because he was said to have filmed the incident, Mediapart and AFP report. The BBC has contacted his agent and the Paris prosecutor's office for comment.

Nicloux told Mediapart that the scene had been improvised and he had not intervened as he had not observed "any constraints, verbal or physical opposition, or even discomfort".

The site published production documents showing footage of the scene had been destroyed.

The actress told the outlet that she had told friends, her agent and others involved in the film's production in Normandy about the incident at the time, but only filed the complaint after other women accused Depardieu of sexual misconduct.

The Asterix and Obelix star will next week find out whether he will stand trial for allegedly raping another actress, Charlotte Arnould.

On Monday, Depardieu dropped his appeal against a separate conviction for two counts of sexual assault during another film shoot, for which he was handed an 18-month suspended sentence.

Several other women have made allegations against the 77-year-old in the media.

articles.title: Trump threatens ban on US firms building AI data centres overseas
articles.summary: The US president provided little detail on the potential policy, saying others in his team were hearing about it for the first time.
articles.body:
Donald Trump has said he will ban US companies from building AI data centres overseas, threatening a "tremendous tax" for tech firms who do so.

"We're going to keep it all in this country," the US president said, while providing little detail on the potential policy he said others in his cabinet were hearing about for the first time.

Data centres were a central issue in the midterm elections earlier in November, with many Democratic candidates promising tougher regulation on their construction.

Tech giants including Meta and Google have entered agreements to build data centres overseas. It remains unclear how such a policy would be enforced if it was brought in.

"We're not going to allow our companies to build data centres outside of our country," Trump told reporters in a press briefing following his return from his trip to Asia.

"Because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen."

But whether that idea will become policy remains unclear.

"I don't know if that's a breaking story, but I haven't even said that to my people. But I'm telling them now, they're here," he said.

Trump floated the policy after saying the US was leading on data centre construction, and he would not allow China to beat the US when it came to AI - which he calls super intelligence, or SI.

It also follows an announcement earlier this week that would restrict the export of advanced computer chips and who can access the computing power provided by them.

Washington on Monday announced firms would require a licence to buy advanced chips, so US officials can monitor whether they are being used to serve Chinese companies or they are being smuggled into China.

The move will impact South East Asian countries that have invested heavily in data centres, as Chinese companies seek to rent computing power from overseas.

Why Canada is embracing AI data centres while the US pushes back

Data centres are crucial to the AI boom. The vast warehouse-style buildings house the advanced computer chips and servers that are needed to run AI programmes such as Claude and ChatGPT.

As of April there were about 3,000 data centres across the US, with another 1,500 in various stages of approval and construction, according to the Pew Research Centre.

Many of them are built in rural areas, and concerns about issues including noise pollution and energy consumption helped drive Democratic candidates promising tougher rules on data centre construction to wins on 3 November.

"You ought to take advantage of the data centres. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but take advantage don't shut them off," Trump said.

"We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they're great places. They have energy and they have everything. They're tremendous assets."

Large tech firms - often called AI hyperscalers due to the size of their investments in AI - have also been branching out, and Canada has made moves to step in to offer itself as an alternative location for these sites, with less local pushback against projects so far.

Meta has already broken ground on a data centre in the province of Alberta, and Anthropic has signed a long-term agreement to lease a proposed data centre in Nova Scotia.

The BBC has reached out to Meta for comment on Trump's remarks.

In September Google announced a €13bn ($15bn: £11bn) investment in AI infrastructure in Finland, which included funding for three data centres.

Last month, building work for two of those centres was halted due to concerns over the clearance of more than 300 hectares of forest.

Trump called out the build in Finland specifically, saying his administration was "not allowing that to happen".

articles.title: Palestinian anti-Hamas groups accused of role in Israel Gaza operation
articles.summary: Israeli-backed Palestinian militias accused of expanding operations, raising concerns over their role in Gaza’s security
articles.body:
Nuseirat refugee camp, Gaza Strip – It was late on Tuesday evening when a group of armed men stopped outside a house sheltering displaced Palestinian women on ad-Dawa Street, on the northern edge of the Nuseirat refugee camp in central Gaza.

The streets were gradually emptying, and drones could be heard overhead. The men wore no military uniforms or insignia. They were Palestinians in civilian clothes carrying light weapons, believed to be members of Israeli-backed local militias, locals said.

The gunmen surrounded the house and forced the women into the street and questioned them by torchlight about a man they were looking for. They threatened those who refused to answer and fired into the air before withdrawing minutes later without detaining anyone.

Hours later, on Wednesday, the Israeli military launched a ground operation near the Nuseirat and Bureij refugee camps, west of the so-called “Yellow Line” that demarcates areas under Israeli military control following the October 2025 ceasefire.

The military closed Salah al-Din Street, Gaza’s main north-south thoroughfare. About 6,000 Palestinians fled, according to Gaza’s Government Media Office.

Israel said the operation targeted a tunnel that posed a threat to its troops. On Thursday, the military said that the operation had been completed. At least one Palestinian was killed in Israeli attacks near where the incursion took place.

The sequence of events raises questions about the extent of coordination between Israeli forces and Palestinian armed groups, whose activities have expanded across Gaza in recent weeks.

A Palestinian security source in Gaza told Al Jazeera that security authorities had documented the local armed groups’ participation in this week’s Israeli military operation in central Gaza.

Their activities included “terrorising civilians and pressuring families to evacuate homes and shelters”, the source said.

Speaking on condition of anonymity, the source said the groups benefitted from Israeli military fire cover and the closure of Salah al-Din Street, which also impeded humanitarian operations.

The source described them as “gangs”, financed and armed by Israel to undermine Palestinian internal cohesion by “engineering chaos”.

Israel has publicly acknowledged supporting armed groups opposed to Hamas in Gaza, as it fought its genocidal war on the Palestinian enclave, killing more than 74,000 people. “What’s wrong with that?” asked Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu last year, claiming that the policy had saved the lives of Israeli soldiers.

Expanding military and intelligence roles

Palestinian political analyst Iyad al-Qarra told Al Jazeera that Israel had expanded the armed groups’ reach from Rafah and Khan Younis in the south to central Gaza and Gaza City.

He accused the groups of carrying out kidnappings and attempted assassinations targeting Palestinians, including members of Palestinian factions, in which they benefitted from Israeli aerial protection and fire cover.

Al-Qarra linked their expanding activities to Israel’s demolition of buildings and forced displacement of Palestinians, which have enabled the groups to operate in areas that Israeli forces would otherwise struggle to access.

He said the Israeli military uses the fighters in front-line operations before committing its own troops.

The groups also gather intelligence through local social and family networks while receiving information from the Israeli military, al-Qarra said.

Who are the Israeli-backed anti-Hamas groups?

The groups emerged during Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, with some accused of looting aid supplies before taking on broader roles through Israeli funding, weapons and coordination with the military and intelligence services.

Published estimates point to about five main groups with several hundred members in total. In April, the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED) monitor reported that Israel had increased its support for them, including deploying attack drones during their clashes with Hamas.

The groups include the Popular Forces in Rafah, led by Ghassan al-Duhaini, since founder Yasser Abu Shabab was killed in December 2025; Hussam al-Astal’s group east of Khan Younis; and Shawqi Abu Nuseira’s group in central Gaza.

Two others, led by Rami Helles and Ashraf al-Mansi, operate in eastern Gaza City and northern Gaza, respectively.

Palestinian political analyst Wesam Afifa told Al Jazeera that Israel seeks to establish local security influence that it could retain even after a partial military withdrawal.

He cited Israel’s historical support for the South Lebanon Army before its withdrawal from Lebanon in 2000, and more limited forms of collaboration during the first and second Palestinian Intifadas.

What distinguishes the situation in Gaza, Afifa said, is the groups’ transition from limited support roles to conducting armed operations outside areas under direct Israeli military control.

He pointed to their involvement in searching and obstructing travellers returning through the Rafah border crossing, which he said contradicted existing agreements and the role of the European Union monitoring mission.

In February, the United Nations Human Rights Office documented accounts from Palestinian returnees alleging intimidation, searches and theft by armed Palestinians purportedly backed by Israel.

Afifa warned that the groups’ continued presence could extend Israeli security influence beyond a military withdrawal, raising the possibility that Israel could push for their inclusion in Gaza’s future security arrangements.

articles.title: US feels like a golden prison: Google engineer on H-1B visa says he's moving to the UK without a job, says he hasn't traveled outside US for 18 months out of fear
articles.summary: Yash Sharma, a 36-year-old Indian software engineer working at Google in San Francisco, has decided to move to the UK even though he does not have a job
articles.body: Yash Sharma, a 36-year-old Indian software engineer working at Google in San Francisco, has decided to move to the UK even though he does not have a job there. But the visa uncertainties in the US have become unbearable. After spending six years on an H-1B visa, Sharma has decided to leave the US and move to the UK next month, he said to Bloomberg News. He described the US as a "golden prison", saying that the constant changes to immigration rules, limited prospects of obtaining permanent residency and fear of being unable to return after travelling abroad have taken a toll on his professional and personal life.Sharma said he had become increasingly discouraged about his chances of converting his temporary work visa into permanent residency because of the enormous Green Card backlog facing Indian nationals. He has not travelled outside the US for 18 months because he fears he may not be allowed to return. As a result, he has missed family visits, professional conferences and trips with friends. He also explored an alternative immigration route by applying for an extraordinary ability visa, which is intended for individuals with exceptional achievements in their professional fields. But his application was rejected after months of waiting.Sharma started exploring options outside the US and applied for the UK's Global Talent visa and received approval. The visa allows him to relocate to Britain without having secured a job beforehand and search for employment after arriving. "I've seen various administrations, and to me it's clear that there will be no actual change to the law," Sharma said."The US feels like a golden prison," he said.Trump's H-1B crackdown adds to uncertaintyTrump's immigration crackdown began shortly after he returned to the White House in January 2025. While the administration initially focused on illegal immigration, its policies increasingly extended to legal immigration programmes, including the H-1B system used by American companies to recruit highly skilled foreign professionals.In September 2025, Trump announced a $100,000 payment requirement for certain new H-1B workers seeking to enter the US from abroad.The administration argued that the programme had been abused by employers who used lower-paid foreign workers instead of hiring American employees. The changes have created additional uncertainty for companies that depend on international talent, particularly in the technology sector.The administration has also introduced a wage-weighted H-1B selection system, giving applicants offered higher prevailing wages better chances of being selected in the visa lottery.For workers already in the US, the difficulties extend beyond obtaining an H-1B visa. Long waits for employment-based green cards, visa stamping delays and uncertainty over future immigration rules have made long-term planning increasingly difficult.IBM ends visa sponsorship for most consulting jobsAmerican companies are also changing their approach to foreign hiring. IBM told employees this month that it would discontinue visa and green card sponsorship for the majority of positions in its IBM Consulting division. The affected employees have been given the option of continuing their work for the company from locations outside the US or leaving IBM by the end of the year.Soon after IBM, Boston-based financial technology company Flywire announced they were also evaluating how immigration restrictions could affect its workforce and business operations.The company processes billions of dollars in payments every month for colleges and other clients. In its quarterly filing this month, Flywire said it was considering shifting hiring and product development activities to lower-cost countries where it already operates to offset rising immigration-related expenses. The company warned that difficulties in recruiting and retaining specialised employees could slow product development.Chris Thomas, an immigration lawyer and partner at Holland & Hart in Denver, told Bloomberg that corporate clients were concerned that even an inadvertent compliance mistake could expose them to government investigations or restrictions on their ability to sponsor foreign workers.Some companies are questioning whether navigating the increasingly complicated immigration system is worth the effort. "Some are saying it's too much, it's time to start offshoring," Thomas said. Kate Angustia, supervisory policy and practice counsel at the American Immigration Lawyers Association, warned that the uncertainty was creating instability across the immigration system. "We are creating a brain drain," she said.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
